title: Krishna
tomorrow: a hunter's arrow hits Krishna. what does Krishna say to him?

segments.voice: Yesterday, one small but: krishnas tu bhagavan svayam, read as the source by some and as Vishnu's full descent by others. Today, Krishna explains in his own voice why he keeps coming.

Some sounds mean it's starting before anyone says a word: the whistle before a game, the first chord at a concert, the kettle about to boil. In the Bhagavad Gita it's conch shells. Two armies face each other, and the conches are blown, one after another, until the noise makes the earth and sky ring. Between the armies, the warrior Arjuna puts down his bow, and his charioteer, Krishna, starts to teach. Partway through, Krishna says he gave this teaching to the sun god long ago. Arjuna asks the obvious thing. How? You were born recently. The sun god came first.
screen: `A SOUND THAT MEANS IT'S STARTING.` → `CONCHES BETWEEN TWO ARMIES.` → `HOW CAN YOU BE THAT OLD?`

segments.voice: This is the fourth chapter of the Gita, and Krishna answers in layers. First: you and I have both been born many times, Arjuna. I remember them all; you don't. Then something stranger. I am unborn and undying, the Lord of all beings, and still, through my own power, I come into being. Unborn, and born anyway. Then the two verses that sound like the whole series of descents explaining itself. Whenever dharma declines and its opposite rises, Krishna says, I send myself forth. To protect the good, to undo those who do harm, and to set dharma firmly in place again, I come into being age after age. In Sanskrit, that last phrase is sambhavami yuge yuge. Listen to it: yuge yuge, age, age. The word repeats the way the coming repeats. So the answer to Arjuna isn't a birthday. It's a rhythm: when the world tips over, he comes, and he has come before. Lay it over the forms so far. The fish in the flood. The boar lifting the earth out of the waters. The man-lion at the doorway. The dwarf and his three steps. Each one arrives when something has slipped. The Gita names that rhythm from the inside, in the voice of the one who keeps arriving.
screen: `BORN MANY TIMES. I REMEMBER.` · `UNBORN, AND BORN ANYWAY.` · `WHENEVER DHARMA SLIPS.` · `YUGE YUGE: AGE AFTER AGE.` · then, large: `THE COMING REPEATS.`

segments.voice: Choose one sound that keeps coming back where you are: a clock, traffic, a fan, your own breath. Listen to it for the whole sit, and hear each return as if it were the first. When your mind drifts, the next return of the sound is your way back.
Krishna: the charioteer of the Gita, who says that whenever dharma slips, he comes, age after age.
For the road: Krishna, who comes not once but yuge yuge, age after age, whenever dharma slips. Until tomorrow.

fork.setup: your school club fixes the same broken thing every year, and someone sighs: why bother, it'll just break again. what does Krishna's rhythm say?
options: coming back to set it right, again and again, is the point, not a failure.
fix it once, perfectly, and you should never have to deal with it again.
if something keeps breaking, it was never really worth fixing at all.
fork.reveal: Krishna says he comes whenever dharma slips, age after age. In this picture, setting things right is never a one-time job.
